problems.description: tasks table omits a user_id foreign key while every sibling table (users, items) is user-scoped; tasks are globally visible, diverging from the established data-model pattern
Title required/empty/whitespace validation is duplicated between create_task and update_task instead of being shared

Measured convention score 0.67 flags 9 violations, but 7 are in untouched files (celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py, repositories.py) and the app.py/test_tasks.py 'Classes should use PascalCase' hits are pre-existing since the diff adds +0 classes — the commit itself is clean snake_case
No validation or test that arbitrary status strings (e.g. 'banana') are rejected; any value is persisted without an allowed-status check

strengths: Follows the existing Blueprint architecture exactly: url_prefix, register_blueprint, and the auth/items/admin section-header comment style
Reuses established get_db() and jsonify() idioms consistently across all five endpoints
Comprehensive test suite: 20 tests covering success, validation, 404s, ordering, and no-op updates
Idempotent schema addition via CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS, matching init_db conventions
Clean diff: +215 lines, no bugs, no duplications, all snake_case
commit_reviews.summary: A well-structured greenfield feature that faithfully mirrors the app's Blueprint/JSON/sqlite patterns with strong tests, though it introduces a minor data-model inconsistency (tasks not user-scoped) and the measured 0.67 convention score reflects mostly pre-existing violations in files untouched by this diff, not the commit itself.

problems.description: Legacy `tokens` table is still created in init_db() but is now dead code after the swap to JWT; leftover schema should be removed for cleanliness.
migrate_tasks_owner_id() runs a PRAGMA column check on every init_db() call; harmless but could be guarded or run once.
JWT payload carries role/username; role changes in the DB are not reflected until token expiry, so permissions can go stale.

Convention score of 0.67 is driven by violations in files outside this commit's diff (celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py, repositories.py); the commit's own code (app.py, test_tasks.py) is internally consistent, so the measurement over-penalizes this diff.

strengths: Replaces insecure static-salt SHA256 hashing with werkzeug's generate_password_hash/check_password_hash.
Fixes the login flow: previously compared hashes inside SQL; now queries by username and verifies with check_password_hash.
Adds per-user task ownership with a real FOREIGN KEY and scopes all task queries/deletes by owner_id.
Wraps task endpoints with the existing require_auth decorator instead of hand-rolling auth per route, respecting the established pattern.
Adds auth helpers and tests (register_and_login, auth_headers) expanding coverage of the new flow.
Net -3 SonarQube smells and removes now-unused imports (hashlib, time).
commit_reviews.summary: Coherent feature_addition that moves from opaque-token to JWT auth and adds proper per-user task ownership, with good security improvements, though it leaves the old tokens table behind as minor dead schema and the 0.67 convention score reflects pre-existing violations outside this diff.

problems.description: send_notification_email is a print() stub rather than real email delivery, and its user_email parameter receives a username (user['username']), creating a latent correctness/maintainability mismatch once real sending is wired up.
Adds a hard Celery + Redis runtime dependency imported at module load in app.py with no dependency/requirements or config file update in this commit; app will fail to start without Celery installed.
New celery_config.py and celery_tasks.py introduce module-level config values in snake_case/lowercase and trigger convention violations, driving convention score to 0.67.
Notification trigger is coupled directly inside update_task rather than via a post-commit/event hook, so the async-email concern is not fully decoupled from the task-update handler.

strengths: Appropriate architectural choice: backgrounding notification via a Celery task queue routed to a dedicated 'email' queue decouples side effects from the request/response path.
Clean separation of Celery app (celery_tasks.py) and configuration (celery_config.py) with sensible defaults via env vars.
Strong testing: 5 tests cover trigger-on-complete, non-trigger on other statuses, title-only updates, combined updates, and the not-found path, all via mocked .delay().
SonarQube delta is net positive: -2 smells, +0 bugs, +0 duplications.
Integration matches existing app.py structure (blueprints, helpers, jsonify responses).
commit_reviews.summary: Solid, well-tested async notification integration that improves the architecture, but it ships a print() placeholder with a username-as-email mismatch and undeclared dependencies; note that the 0.67 convention score is likely overstated by linter noise (PascalCase violations listed despite +0 classes, and a hit on untouched repositories.py) while the +91 cognitive-complexity jump appears inflated for only 6 simple functions.

problems.description: SonarQube reports +20 cognitive complexity and +7 smells for a commit described as a pure refactor, meaning the new repository layer added complexity rather than netting it out.
Convention score is 0.67 with 9 violations: repositories.py module-level constants are not UPPER_CASE, and classes in test_tasks.py, celery_config.py, and celery_tasks.py are not PascalCase.

Introduces a repository pattern that did not previously exist (inline SQL in handlers), so it does not respect the established pattern; it is an intentional new layering that may be inconsistent until the migration completes.

strengths: Centralizes SQL in repository classes, removing duplicated SELECT column lists and query strings across handlers (e.g., the repeated tasks projection).
Preserves endpoint behavior exactly: find_by_username, create_item returning lastrowid as item_id, and ownership-scoped lookups all carry the same semantics.
Repos are instantiated per request with the active connection, which is transaction-safe and keeps the boundary explicit.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid, behavior-preserving migration of inline SQL into a repository layer that improves maintainability, though the measured +7 smells/+20 complexity and 0.67 convention score (largely driven by files outside the visible app.py portion of the diff) indicate the refactor adds some debt and the new pattern intentionally diverges from the prior inline-SQL style.

problems.description: Adds flask_limiter import (4 new imports) but the diff shows no requirements.txt update — the new dependency is undeclared, so deploys/pipelines will fail to import app.

RATE_LIMIT_STORAGE defaults to a hardcoded redis://localhost:6379/2; if Redis is down or unreachable, every request fails rather than degrading gracefully, and the infra coupling is implicit rather than injected.

count_tasks_by_owner() runs a full COUNT(*) scan on every paginated list request, adding an O(n) pass on the hot path; keyset pagination with has_more from limit+1 already knows completeness without a total.

get_rate_limit_key() decodes the JWT on every request, duplicating the decode already done by @require_auth; IP fallback will bucket all users together behind a reverse proxy unless PROXY_FIX is configured.

next_cursor is serialized as a string but the query param is parsed as int — a response/request type inconsistency clients must round-trip; also the 100-iteration rate-limit loops are brittle against fixed-window boundary resets (mitigated by the reset fixture).
SonarQube cognitive complexity +23 — the nested try/except key_func and the pagination branching logic raise complexity; extraction of the pagination cursor logic would contain it.

strengths: Keyset (cursor) pagination with stable created_at DESC, id DESC ordering and limit+1 has_more detection — no offset drift and consistent tiebreak ordering.
Rate limiting keyed per authenticated user via JWT sub with IP fallback, giving genuine user isolation (verified by test).
Thorough tests: response shape, ordering, cross-user isolation, 429 + Retry-After, per-user limit isolation, and an autouse limiter.reset() fixture.
Matches existing file conventions — comment banners, repository-method pattern, env-driven config with memory:// override for tests.
commit_reviews.summary: Solid, well-tested addition of user-keyed rate limiting and cursor pagination that fits the existing repository/route patterns, but ships an undeclared flask-limiter dependency and a hardcoded Redis storage default, and the 0.67 convention score is largely pre-existing (most flagged violations are in untouched files).

compounding_issues: Session 1 added the tasks feature without authentication or ownership, forcing Session 2 to retrofit an owner_id column via a runtime ALTER TABLE migration (migrate_tasks_owner_id) and a leftover stub migration helper (_run_migration_v1)

Session 1's opaque DB-stored token scheme was replaced wholesale by JWTs in Session 2, stranding dead code: the tokens table is still created in init_db and the static-salt SHA256 hashing was swapped for werkzeug, all mid-stream rework
Session 5's cursor pagination orders by created_at DESC, id DESC but paginates on id < cursor alone, so rows with mismatched id/created_at ordering could be skipped or duplicated in edge cases
key_decisions: Moving from DB-stored opaque tokens to stateless JWT (pyjwt) with werkzeug password hashing in Session 2, which unlocked per-user rate-limiting keys in Session 5
Adding owner_id ownership scoping to tasks in Session 2 with an idempotent ALTER TABLE migration, making all task endpoints auth-gated and user-isolated
Integrating Celery for async completion notifications in Session 3, decoupling email side-effects from request handlers via a delay() seam that tests can mock
Extracting a repository layer (BaseRepository + User/Task/Items repos) in Session 4, removing raw SQL from app.py and enabling clean cursor-paginated queries in Session 5
Adding flask_limiter rate limiting keyed by JWT subject in Session 5, using memory:// storage in tests to avoid a Redis dependency
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily across all five sessions. The test suite grew monotonically (16 to 28 to 33 to 33 to 46 tests) and every commit was fully green, so each session landed without regressions while layering on new capability: Session 2 hardened Session 1's unauthenticated tasks with JWT auth and ownership, Session 3 added Celery integration, Session 4 refactored toward a repository pattern, and Session 5 capped the arc with rate limiting and pagination. The main blemish is that early-session decisions (unauthenticated tasks, opaque tokens) had to be reworked rather than planned, leaving migration scaffolding and a dead tokens table behind, though the refactor in Session 4 demonstrates the codebase was healthy enough to structurally absorb new features cleanly.
story_review.summary: A textbook greenfield-to-cross-cutting progression that delivered continuous, test-verified improvement, marred only by early authentication and ownership decisions that had to be retrofitted later.
